transcript.text: We had a power cut last night and now our Candy washer dryer is completely dead - no lights, nothing. Everything else in the house came back on. The plug fuse is fine, I swapped it. Help!

A total loss of lights/display after a power cut usually means the washer dryer is not receiving mains power, or the power cut/surge has damaged its internal mains filter/power board. It is unlikely to be a normal door-lock or programme fault.

Try these safe checks first:

1. Check the wall socket itself
• Plug in a lamp, phone charger, or another known-working appliance.
• Check any nearby wall switch is on.
• Check your consumer unit/fuse board for a tripped RCD/MCB — sometimes only the socket circuit has tripped even though other things in the house work.

2. Fully power-reset the machine
• Switch it off at the wall and unplug it.
• Leave it unplugged for 10–15 minutes.
• While unplugged, hold the washer dryer’s On/Off button for around 15 seconds.
• Plug it directly back into a known-good wall socket and try again.

3. Check the plug/cable externally
• You have already changed the fuse — ensure it is the correct type/rating, normally a 13 A BS1362 fuse for a washer dryer.
• Inspect the lead and plug for scorching, looseness, melted plastic, or a burnt smell.
• Do not use an extension lead or multiway adaptor for testing.

4. If the socket works but the machine remains entirely dead
• Unplug it and stop there. Do not remove the top/back panels.
• A cut/restoration can take out the washer dryer’s mains interference filter, an internal fuse/thermal protection component, or the control PCB/power supply. Those faults commonly produce exactly “no lights, no response.”

If there was a bang, burning smell, smoke, visible damage, or it trips the circuit breaker when plugged in, keep it disconnected and arrange service urgently.

Given that the plug fuse has been replaced and it is still completely lifeless, the most likely next step is a Candy-approved engineer or a competent appliance repairer. Tell them: “Machine completely dead immediately after a power cut; wall socket and plug fuse checked.” That helps point them toward the mains input filter/power board rather than the motor or door lock.

If you give me the exact Candy model number (usually inside the door opening or on the back), plus whether the wall socket tests live, I can narrow down the likely fault and whether the machine has any accessible reset.

Socket's fine, a lamp works in it. I've also unplugged it for over 10 minutes and tried again, still dead. The model is CSOW 4965TWE/1-80. Plug and lead look fine, no burnt smell. So is it the engineer route then?

Yes — with a known-good socket, good plug fuse, intact lead, and a proper power reset, this has moved beyond user checks. Arrange an appliance engineer.

For that Candy CSOW 4965TWE/1-80, the likely fault is in the incoming power path or electronics, such as:

• internal mains/RFI filter
• internal wiring connection or thermal fuse
• control-module power supply / main PCB

A voltage transient when power was restored can cause a failure like this, even without a smell, bang, or visible damage.

What to do now:

1. Leave it unplugged until it is inspected.
2. Contact Candy/Haier service if it may still be under the manufacturer warranty, or use a reputable independent white-goods engineer if not.
3. Give them the exact symptom:
   “Candy CSOW 4965TWE/1-80 completely dead after a power cut. Socket tested working, plug fuse changed/tested, machine unplugged/reset, no lights or response.”
4. Have the serial number from the rating plate ready (usually inside the door opening or on the rear).

Before authorising an expensive repair, ask for a diagnostic/fixed-price quote. If it is only the mains filter or an internal supply component, it may be a relatively straightforward repair; if the main PCB has failed, costs can be substantially higher.

If the cut affected other electrical items, take photos/notes and check your home insurance policy for “electrical damage” or power-surge cover — though the excess can make a single appliance claim uneconomic.
